title: Strongest El Niño in 70 Years Drives Global Food Prices to Highest Since 2022
excerpt: The UN weather agency says El Niño will persist through February 2027 with near certainty, as FAO data shows food commodity prices climbing across every major category.
body:
• The World Meteorological Organization says 2026's El Niño is on track to be the strongest in at least 70 years, with near 100% probability of persisting through February 2027.
  • The FAO Food Price Index rose to 133.3 in August — its highest since November 2022 — as cereals, sugar, vegetable oils, meat, and dairy all climbed.
  • Corn prices are up 33% from their late-June low and sugar has risen 23% from its late-July low, driven by weather disruption and Black Sea shipping constraints.
  • The World Food Programme estimates El Niño could push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by end of 2027.

The United Nations has issued its starkest warning yet about the current El Niño event, with the World Meteorological Organization declaring it on track to become the strongest in at least 70 years. Pacific Ocean temperatures in parts of the tropics exceeded normal levels by more than eight degrees Celsius in July and August — four times the threshold that defines a very strong El Niño.

"The question is no longer whether El Niño will strengthen, but how much heat — and disruption — it will leave behind," said Celeste Saulo, head of the WMO. The agency said the likelihood of El Niño persisting through February 2027 is now close to 100%, a level of certainty it has never before expressed for an El Niño forecast.

Food Prices Climbing Across the Board

The economic impact is already materializing. The FAO Food Price Index, which tracks monthly changes in a basket of internationally traded food commodities, averaged 133.3 points in August, up from 130.8 in July and the highest reading since November 2022. Every major food category — cereals, vegetable oils, sugar, meat, and dairy — recorded increases.

"The risk premium is returning to food markets: climate shocks, geopolitical tensions, and disrupted trade logistics are converging to tighten supply expectations."

— Maximo Torero, FAO Chief Economist

Corn prices have surged roughly 33% from their late-June low, driven by El Niño-related concerns about South American production and ongoing disruption to Black Sea grain shipments from the Ukraine-Russia conflict. Sugar is up approximately 23% from its late-July low, with lower production in Brazil's center-south region compounding weather worries across Asia and Europe.

The FAO also cut its 2026 global cereal production forecast by 3.4 million metric tons to 2.98 billion tons, the largest annual decline since 2018. While that figure still represents the second-highest production on record, projected world cereal stocks were revised down to 947.2 million tons — only marginally above the previous season.

India Faces Direct Impact

El Niño's effects are projected to hit India particularly hard. Below-normal monsoon rainfall threatens sugar and rice production, two of the country's most critical crops both domestically and for export markets. India is the world's largest sugar producer and second-largest rice producer, and any significant shortfall could ripple through global commodity markets.

Across South and Southeast Asia more broadly, the WMO forecasts drought risks, uneven monsoons, and localized flooding that could disrupt agricultural production through the winter growing season.

Hunger Crisis Deepens

Beyond commodity markets, the human toll is mounting. The World Food Programme estimates that a strong El Niño could push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity across 45 vulnerable countries, raising the total to 274 million — a 22% increase over current levels. Central America and Southern Africa face the sharpest projected increases, at 83% and 75% respectively.

"These are events that in the past have triggered large-scale hunger," said Jean-Martin Bauer, director of WFP's food security analysis service.

The crisis is compounded by geopolitical disruptions. Escalating attacks in the Black Sea have curtailed grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, while the U.S.-Iran conflict is straining global fertilizer supply chains. European harvests of corn and sugar beet have also been damaged by extreme heat and drought.

"Never before has the UN weather agency issued such an unequivocal forecast for El Niño or its cooler counterpart, La Niña."

— World Meteorological Organization

Analysts at Rabobank and Barclays have flagged the weather system as a significant driver of commodity market volatility, with further price increases likely as El Niño approaches its expected peak in the coming months. For consumers and policymakers worldwide, the convergence of extreme weather, conflict, and strained supply chains presents a food security challenge not seen since the aftermath of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
